newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Deng's legacy to Hong Kong - prosperity.
newsitem.headline: Deng's legacy to Hong Kong - prosperity.

text.p: There can be few places in the world more finely tuned to the state of health of China's elderly paramount leader Deng Xiaoping than the British colony of Hong Kong.

Hong Kong, though tiny, is the world's eighth largest trading economy but the financial colossus found it impossible to cut the ties which anchored it to the vital signs on a hospital chart of the diminutive 92-year-old veteran, who died late on Wednesday and was not seen in public for three years.
In recent days, rumours of his impending demise battered the markets but, tellingly, there was no repeat of the wild plunges seen in the 1980s.

In the past, even a hint of a rumour that he was on his deathbed had been enough to send the wealthy community of six million people into a funk, wiping millions of dollars off the stock market in minutes.
But the absence of market over-reaction in recent days to news that he was sinking fast was vindication of Deng's legacy to Hong Kong.
With less than five months to go until the handover to China, Hong Kong is able to look forward without any marked degree of panic of reunification with a China without Deng.

"His disappearance from the scene will have no real impact on how the last few weeks of the countdown will proceed," said Richard Margolis, a former British diplomat involved in the Sino-British negotiations on the return of Hong Kong and now a first vice president of equity research at Merrill Lynch. Hong Kong, a British colony for over 150 years, reverts to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
Deng will now never achieve his ambition of seeing Hong Kong, wrested from China at gunpoint by the British as spoils of victory in the opium wars, return to the fold.
But his ghost will no doubt hover over the ceremonies when the British flag is furled for the last time and China's red flag rises over Hong Kong.
It was Deng who was credited with formulating the one country, two systems formula which made it possible for the Britain to agree to return Hong Kong to China.
Hong Kong's freedoms, its capitalist liftstyle honed under decades under the Union jack would prevail for 50 years.
It was the second plank of his policy -- of gradually opening up an isolated China to the world's markets -- which sealed the bargain in Hong Kong eyes.
Hong Kong entrepreneurs began to venture into a China many had fled in panic from the totalitarian advance of communism barely a generation earlier.

Hong Kong money and Deng's reforms have narrowed the gulf between Hong Kong and southern China, sweeping away fears that Hong Kong would drown in a bottomless pit of poverty. Instead, both Hong Kong and China prospered in tandem.

The reforms Deng unleashed have gone so far that the fears which Hong Kong harboured in the early 1980s have disappeared. Hong Kong people no longer fear that Deng's death would allow the hardliners back in and send the bamboo curtain crashing down again.

"The key fact is that the reforms Deng was the architect of have unleashed social and economic forces that are the determining factors of what happens now rather than individual personalities," Margolis said.

"Ultimately Deng does not factor into the equation any more in terms of China's relationship with Hong Kong. (His death) is more of a symbolic event," said Andrew Fernow, director of research at stockbrokers Vickers Ballas.
